cards.title: CCP Veritas
cards.body: CCP Veritas, of CCP's Team Gridlock, was not trying to make huge fights fast, but to make overload behave. The stated goal: the server 'should degrade in such a way that the queue of tasklets waiting for execution is minimized - ideally zero.' Slow the clock, keep the queue empty.
cards.prompt: In 2011 an EVE server engineer wrote that the war on lag cannot be won, because players can always bring one more ship. What did the blog propose the server do instead when it falls behind, and what was the stated goal of that behaviour?
cards.answer: Time Dilation - slow the game clock inside the overloaded solar system so the queue of waiting tasklets stays near zero. Graceful degradation, not more speed.

cards.title: The Bloodbath of B-R5RB
cards.body: The corp holding sovereignty for Pandemic Legion left its bill on auto-pay unchecked, and B-R5RB lapsed. 7,548 pilots landed on a killmail, 6,058 fought in system, 2,670 at peak, over 21 hours. Destroyed: 75 titans, 13 supercarriers, 370 dreadnoughts, 123 carriers - 11 trillion ISK, roughly $300,000-$330,000.
cards.prompt: One missed automatic payment in January 2014 opened a dead-end EVE solar system to capture. How many pilots ended up fighting inside that single system, and what did the wreckage come to in real money?
cards.answer: 6,058 fought inside B-R5RB with 2,670 in system at peak (7,548 pilots across the whole battle); 11 trillion ISK destroyed, about $300,000-$330,000 on CCP's own PLEX conversion.

cards.title: Introducing Time Dilation (TiDi)
cards.body: The design document, written before the feature existed. Under overload 'there's painfully few options. They boil down to two: reduce load or increase processing capacity.' Multi-threading is the only capacity option it names, and it buys 'never as much as most people think'. So CCP reduced load: slow the clock. It ends on the limit, not the win.
cards.prompt: Time Dilation has a published design document you can still open. Name it, its author and its year - and the two options it says an overloaded server actually has.
cards.answer: 'Introducing Time Dilation (TiDi)', CCP Veritas, 22 April 2011. The two options: reduce load, or increase processing capacity.

cards.title: The key that cannot be cut
cards.body: Salting assumes the pieces under a key are independent - N counters that add up. EVE's key holds a fight: mutual visibility and ordering live inside it, so there is no N. That is why CCP spent the clock instead. Run the same check before every split you propose.
cards.prompt: EVE's answer to one overloaded solar system was to slow its clock, never to spread the system over more machines. What property of the data under that key made the split illegal - and what test does that give you before you salt a hot key of your own?
cards.answer: Everything in a solar system must see everything else, in order, so a split buys no fight at all. The test: salting is legal only when the parts sum independently and their order does not matter. A like counter passes; a chat room, an order book or a game tick does not.
